Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple JetBrains IDE plugins caught stealing AI keys

Aikido
2026-06-16 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A coordinated campaign of at least 15 JetBrains IDE plugins, published under seven vendor accounts, exfiltrates the AI provider API key you paste into their settings. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
IPs39.107.60.51

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin ID present in IDE plugins folder · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 AICommand & Control Medium
JetBrains IDEs run plugins inside the IDE's JVM, so a direct outbound connection from idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe to the hardcoded attacker IP 39.107.60.51 is a high-fidelity indicator that one of the 15 malicious AI-assistant plugins has just exfiltrated a stored AI provider API key. The IP is single-purpose and sits in Alibaba Cloud (AS37963) with no legitimate use case for a developer endpoint. Rationale: 39.107.60.51 is the hardcoded plaintext-HTTP exfil server named verbatim in the Aikido write-up (Block 3 / IoC list). A single hit from a developer endpoint is sufficient — no other legitimate caller has been observed for this address.
ATT&CKT1041 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher manually probing the C2 from a sandboxed dev VM
  • Outbound proxy / firewall liveness check explicitly configured to ping the published IOC
  • Sinkhole / decoy traffic from a deliberate honeypot deployment
  • Defender / EDR re-detonation of an archived malicious plugin during retro-hunt
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / file-event history for the affected host and list every plugin under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins — flag any whose XML plugin id matches the 15 IoCs (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.). Capture the InitiatingProcessAccountUpn — that user typed at least one AI provider API key into the plugin settings. 2) Contain: immediately revoke and rotate any OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow API keys belonging to the user; uninstall the offending plugin and remove its directory; block 39.107.60.51 at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on plugin id across all developer endpoints (DeviceFileEvents FolderPath has 'JetBrains' and 'plugins'); check OpenAI / DeepSeek billing portals for unusual usage in the last 60 days from unfamiliar IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to JetBrains Marketplace Plugin AI-Key Stealer C2
id: 7c5e1c34-9a4b-4f2e-9b1a-2d6c0e7b1c01
description: Detects outbound network connection to 39.107.60.51, the hardcoded C2 used by 15 malicious JetBrains plugins (Aikido 2026-06-16) to exfiltrate user-supplied OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys.
references:

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=39.107.60.51
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header AIActions on Objectives Medium
Where a TLS-inspecting proxy or web gateway records full request URLs and headers, this catches the actual exfil call — POST http://39.107.60.51/api/software/<name> carrying the hardcoded static token X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing the victim's apiKey field. This is the most precise rule possible against the campaign because both the URL path and the token are unique to the malicious plugin codebase. Rationale: Both the URI path /api/software/ AND the destination 39.107.60.51 are taken verbatim from the deobfuscated save() handler in the article (Block 2). Either signal alone is unique to this campaign; together they leave no plausible false positive.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester replaying the published IOC against a sanctioned target
  • Threat-intel platform retrospectively decoding archived sandbox PCAPs
  • Vendor security scanner generating synthetic exfil traffic for control validation
  • Honeypot infrastructure deliberately calling the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP / InitiatingProcessAccountUpn from the POST — that user's stored AI keys are already at the attacker. Identify which JetBrains IDE process (idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe) made the call so the responsible plugin id can be tied back via plugin XML. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate every AI provider key (OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow) associated with that developer; uninstall the offending plugin directory and clear the plugin's settings file; block 39.107.60.51 and any URI containing /api/software/ at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: search 90 days of proxy logs for any prior POST to the same URI; pivot on the static header value 'F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D' in raw proxy capture if header logging is enabled; query AI provider billing dashboards for spend anomalies on the victim's keys.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51" or RemoteUrl has "/api/software/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51" or RequestURL has "/api/software/"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin ID present in IDE plugins folder AIInstallation High
All 15 IoC plugin XML ids (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit, etc.) are distinctive enough that any file write under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins or ~/.config/JetBrains/<IDE>/plugins that contains one of these identifiers is conclusive evidence the host installed a backdoored plugin from the campaign. This catches the install moment regardless of whether the user has yet pasted an AI API key. Rationale: Plugin XML ids are the canonical, unique identifier JetBrains uses to dedupe Marketplace entries; the 15 ids in the article's IoC table are the verbatim package identifiers and will be present on disk in any installed copy (Marketplace install writes them into the plugin's META-INF). High-fidelity with effectively zero collision risk.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1505.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint forensics tool re-reading a quarantined plugin artifact
  • Backup software touching the JetBrains plugins directory and re-emitting filenames
  • Developer manually examining a benign plugin coincidentally named identically (improbable — these ids are squatted attacker-chosen strings)
  • Security inventory scanner enumerating installed plugin metadata
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate every plugin under %APPDATA%\JetBrains (Win) or ~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains (mac) or ~/.config/JetBrains (Linux) on the host; cross-reference plugin.xml id against the 15 IoCs; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for that host to confirm whether 39.107.60.51 was already contacted (key already exfil'd). 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin via JetBrains Plugins UI (Disable → Restart → Remove), then delete the residual directory; rotate any AI provider API keys that user has used in the IDE in the last 90 days; push EDR-level block for the plugin id strings. 3) Hunt: sweep the entire developer fleet with the same query over 60d to find every infected host; cross-reference vendor accounts (CodePilot/mycode, StackSmith/misshewei, CodeCrafter/keteme, CodeWeaver/simpledev, JetCode/skyblue, DailyCode/dialycode, ZenCoder/947cb4c8-5db1-4cf0-8182-0aae7c433bb3) for any future plugin uploads.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FileName has_any (MaliciousPluginIds) or FolderPath has_any (MaliciousPluginIds)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Google Vertex AI SDK Flaw Let Attackers Hijack Model Uploads via Bucket Squatting

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A flaw in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python let an attacker with no access to a victim's project hijack the victim's machine learning model upload and run code inside Google's serving infrastructure. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which found and reported the bug through Google's bug bounty program, calls the technique "Pickle in the Middle" and said it saw no exploitation in the wild.

CVEsCVE-2026-2473
ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] GCS staging bucket created matching <project>-vertex-staging-<region> pattern by external account · [LLM] Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK version (<1.148.0) installed or imported
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI Model.upload writing to GCS bucket outside the caller's project · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vertex AI Model registered with artifact_uri pointing to a non-owned GCS bucket
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cross-project GCS write by Vertex AI serving service-agent (metadata token abuse) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
GCS staging bucket created matching <project>-vertex-staging-<region> pattern by external account AIWeaponization High
Detects bucket-squatting precursor: an external/anomalous GCP account creating a Cloud Storage bucket whose name matches the predictable Vertex AI default staging bucket pattern (`<project-id>-vertex-staging-<region>`) for a project they don't own. This is the foothold step in Unit 42's 'Pickle in the Middle' attack — the attacker must win the name race before the victim's SDK calls Model.upload(). Rationale: Article gives the exact predictable bucket name template `<project>-vertex-staging-<region>` that the unpatched SDK generated. Cross-checked against Unit 42's Pickle-in-the-Middle write-up which also lists this naming convention; bucket names are globally unique so squatting attempts are observable in audit logs. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/release-notes
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1583.004
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cross-team bucket pre-provisioning by a central platform team for a downstream project
  • Migration scripts re-creating buckets in a new project after a project rename
  • Internal red-team / Unit 42-style validation testing
  • Terraform reconciliation where the executing service account's project differs from the bucket's project
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountDisplayName endswith "@yourdomain.com" and IPAddress in ("<corp egress IPs>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the bucket's full ACL and the creator's principal/IP from GCP audit; confirm the prefix project ID is one your org actually owns. Step 2 — Contain: if the creator is external or unrecognised, request Google immediately suspend the bucket via abuse reporting (bucket names cannot be reclaimed otherwise), and notify the project's Vertex AI users to set explicit `staging_bucket` and upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform to ≥1.148.0. Step 3 — Hunt: query Vertex AI Model.upload calls in the affected project for the last 30 days to determine whether any artifacts may already have transited the attacker bucket; rotate any service-agent tokens that may have been exposed and audit BigQuery / GKE access from that tenant.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Cloud Platform", "Google Cloud Storage")
| where ActionType has_any ("storage.buckets.create", "google.storage.buckets.create")
| extend BucketName = tostring(ObjectName)
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|eu|asia|northamerica|southamerica|europe|australia|me)-?[a-z0-9-]*$"
| extend BucketProjectPrefix = tostring(split(BucketName, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerEmail = tostring(AccountDisplayName)
| where AccountObjectId !startswith BucketProjectPrefix and not(CallerEmail has BucketProjectPrefix)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, BucketName, BucketProjectPrefix, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent
let LookbackDays = 7d;
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ServiceName == "storage.googleapis.com"
| where MethodName has "storage.buckets.create"
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(ResourceName).bucket)
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|eu|asia|northamerica|southamerica|europe|australia|me)-?[a-z0-9-]*$"
| extend BucketProjectPrefix = tostring(split(BucketName, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerProject = tostring(parse_json(ResourceLabels).project_id)
| where BucketProjectPrefix != CallerProject
| project TimeGenerated, PrincipalEmail, CallerIpAddress, BucketName, BucketProjectPrefix, CallerProject, UserAgent

Vertex AI Model.upload writing to GCS bucket outside the caller's project AIDelivery High
Detects the moment the vulnerable SDK actually performs the malicious upload: a Vertex AI Model.upload / ModelService.UploadModel call where the resolved staging or artifact bucket is owned by a different GCP project than the caller. This is the smoking-gun signal that bucket squatting succeeded. Rationale: Article states the SDK uploaded model files to whichever account owned the matching bucket name and that the victim's project ID was the predictable name seed. A bucket-vs-caller project mismatch on the upload call is the direct attack signature. CloudAppEvents query now uses only canonical columns (ObjectName, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://github.com/googleapis/python-aiplatform/releases/tag/v1.148.0
ATT&CKT1537 T1195.003
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared org bucket intentionally used as a central staging location across projects
  • CI pipelines that publish artifacts to a dedicated artifacts project rather than the workload project
  • Service accounts impersonating into another project where staging is centralised
  • Cross-project Vertex AI Pipelines where staging_bucket is explicitly set to a sibling project
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountDisplayName has "shared-staging" or AccountDisplayName endswith "@<central-platform-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the bucket owner (gsutil ls -L gs://<bucket>) and the caller's project; if owner ≠ caller and bucket was created in last 14 days by an external principal, treat as confirmed squat. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the calling service-agent's metadata-server tokens (Unit 42 confirmed those tokens reach BigQuery / GKE / model registry across the tenant), force-rotate any Workload Identity bindings, and block egress from Vertex AI serving containers to the attacker bucket. Step 3 — Hunt: list every model artifact uploaded by the caller in the last 30 days, re-hash against the registry, and inspect pickle/joblib files for `__reduce__` / `os.system` markers; pivot to BigQuery audit logs for the same service agent for cross-tenant access attempts.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Cloud Platform", "Google Vertex AI", "Google Cloud Storage")
| where ActionType has_any ("storage.objects.create", "aiplatform.models.upload", "google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel", "Model.upload")
| extend Bucket = tostring(ObjectName)
| where Bucket matches regex @"-vertex-staging-"
| extend BucketProjectPrefix = tostring(split(Bucket, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerEmail = tostring(AccountDisplayName)
| where not(CallerEmail has BucketProjectPrefix)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ActionType, Bucket, BucketProjectPrefix, IPAddress, UserAgent
let LookbackDays = 7d;
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ServiceName in ("aiplatform.googleapis.com", "storage.googleapis.com")
| where MethodName has_any ("UploadModel", "storage.objects.create", "Model.upload")
| extend ArtifactUri = tostring(parse_json(Request).model.artifactUri)
| extend BucketFromUri = extract(@"gs://([^/]+)/", 1, ArtifactUri)
| extend BucketFromObject = tostring(parse_json(ResourceName).bucket)
| extend Bucket = coalesce(BucketFromUri, BucketFromObject)
| where Bucket matches regex @"-vertex-staging-"
| extend BucketProjectPrefix = tostring(split(Bucket, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerProject = tostring(parse_json(ResourceLabels).project_id)
| where BucketProjectPrefix != CallerProject
| project TimeGenerated, PrincipalEmail, CallerProject, Bucket, BucketProjectPrefix, ArtifactUri, CallerIpAddress, MethodName

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK version (<1.148.0) installed or imported AIWeaponization Medium
Inventory detection for the root cause: any host, notebook, or CI runner that still has google-cloud-aiplatform pinned below 1.148.0 is exposed to the Pickle-in-the-Middle flaw. Catches both pip-install events of vulnerable versions and requirements.txt / pyproject.toml drops that reference them. Rationale: Article explicitly names v1.148.0 as the fully patched release, v1.144.0 as the partial fix (uuid4 only), and tested vulnerable versions 1.139.0 / 1.140.0. The version-range check is the direct article string. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/googleapis/python-aiplatform/releases/tag/v1.148.0 • https://github.com/googleapis/python-aiplatform/releases/tag/v1.144.0
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientists in sandbox notebooks installing older SDK to reproduce a tutorial
  • CI matrix testing builds intentionally exercising older library versions
  • Air-gapped environments where 1.148.0 isn't yet mirrored
  • Dependency-pinning tools (pip-compile / poetry lock) regenerating locks from old constraints
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip-compile", "poetry lock", "--dry-run"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host is a workload that calls Vertex AI Model.upload or runs training/notebook jobs; check whether `staging_bucket` is explicitly set in the SDK call (mitigates risk even on vulnerable versions). Step 2 — Contain: push an org-wide pip constraint pinning google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.148.0; rebuild affected container images and notebook environments. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to GCP audit logs for any Model.upload calls from this host in the last 30 days and validate destination bucket ownership matches the caller's project (see related UC).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","poetry.exe","uv.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("google-cloud-aiplatform", "google_cloud_aiplatform")
| extend Version = extract(@"google[-_]cloud[-_]aiplatform[=<>!~]+([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(Version)
| extend parts = split(Version, ".")
| extend major = toint(parts[0]), minor = toint(parts[1]), patch = toint(parts[2])
| where major < 1 or (major == 1 and minor < 148)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Version, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","python.exe","poetry.exe","uv.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("google-cloud-aiplatform", "google_cloud_aiplatform")
| extend Version = extract(@"google[-_]cloud[-_]aiplatform[=<>!~]+([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)", 1, CommandLine)
| where isnotempty(Version)
| extend parts = split(Version, ".")
| extend major = toint(parts[0]), minor = toint(parts[1])
| where major < 1 or (major == 1 and minor < 148)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Version

Vertex AI Model registered with artifact_uri pointing to a non-owned GCS bucket AIInstallation High
Detects the post-upload registry side of the attack: a Model resource created/updated in Vertex AI whose `artifactUri` references a gs:// bucket not owned by the caller's project. If the squat succeeded, the registered model points at the attacker's bucket and pickle/joblib loading inside the serving container will execute attacker code. Rationale: Article describes Vertex AI later loading the swapped model from the staging URI; the registered model artifactUri is the canonical place that URI ends up. Mismatch between artifact-bucket project prefix and caller project is the attack tell. CloudAppEvents query rewritten to use canonical columns and to extract artifactUri from RawEventData rather than the invented BucketProjectToken column. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-registry/import-model
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1554
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Centralised ML platform where artifacts live in a shared registry project distinct from training projects
  • Pre-trained model imports from Google's public model garden buckets (gs://vertex-ai-restricted)
  • Model migrations during a project rename / consolidation
  • Multi-region replicas where the artifact bucket sits in a paired region's central project
Suppression filter
| where not(ArtifactBucket startswith "vertex-ai-restricted" or ArtifactBucket startswith "gs://gcs-public-data" or AccountDisplayName endswith "@<central-ml-platform>.iam.gserviceaccount.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the artifactUri's bucket ACL and creator from GCP audit; compare creation time to the model registration time — if the bucket pre-dates the model by <30 min and was created by an external principal, treat as confirmed. Step 2 — Contain: delete or undeploy the model version, revoke deployed endpoint traffic, rotate the serving-container service-agent's tokens (Unit 42 demonstrated cross-tenant blast radius via the metadata server), and quarantine any container images already pulled from the affected registry. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all DeployedModel resources fed from the suspect bucket, scan BigQuery / GKE / model-registry audit logs for the serving service-agent in the impact window, and run a yara scan over the pulled pickle/joblib payload for `__reduce__` / `subprocess` / metadata-server URLs (169.254.169.254).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Cloud Platform", "Google Vertex AI")
| where ActionType has_any ("aiplatform.models.upload", "google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel", "Model.upload", "aiplatform.models.create")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| extend ArtifactUri = extract(@"""artifactUri""\s*:\s*""(gs://[^""]+)""", 1, Raw)
| extend ArtifactBucket = extract(@"gs://([^/]+)/", 1, ArtifactUri)
| where isnotempty(ArtifactBucket)
| extend ArtifactProjectPrefix = tostring(split(ArtifactBucket, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerEmail = tostring(AccountDisplayName)
| where not(CallerEmail has ArtifactProjectPrefix)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, ArtifactUri, ArtifactBucket, ArtifactProjectPrefix, IPAddress, UserAgent
let LookbackDays = 7d;
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ServiceName == "aiplatform.googleapis.com"
| where MethodName has_any ("UploadModel", "CreateModel", "UpdateModel")
| extend ArtifactUri = tostring(parse_json(Request).model.artifactUri)
| extend ArtifactBucket = extract(@"gs://([^/]+)/", 1, ArtifactUri)
| where isnotempty(ArtifactBucket)
| extend ArtifactProjectPrefix = tostring(split(ArtifactBucket, "-vertex-staging-")[0])
| extend CallerProject = tostring(parse_json(ResourceLabels).project_id)
| where ArtifactProjectPrefix != CallerProject
| project TimeGenerated, PrincipalEmail, CallerProject, ArtifactUri, ArtifactBucket, ArtifactProjectPrefix, CallerIpAddress, MethodName

CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where Change.action IN ("created","modified") Change.object_category="model" by Change.user Change.object Change.dest Change.src

| rex field=dest "gs://(?<artifact_bucket>[^/]+)/"

| eval bucket_project=mvindex(split(artifact_bucket, "-vertex-staging-"), 0) 
| eval caller_project=if(match(user, "@"), mvindex(split(user, "@"), 1), user)

Cross-project GCS write by Vertex AI serving service-agent (metadata token abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the post-compromise blast-radius step Unit 42 demonstrated: the Vertex AI serving container's OAuth token, stolen from the metadata server, was not deployment-scoped and could read model artifacts, BigQuery metadata, and GKE info across the tenant. Catches the serving service-agent making cross-project GCS reads/writes that should never happen in a properly isolated tenant. Rationale: Article: 'the token was not limited to the compromised deployment. It could access other model artifacts in the same Google-managed tenant project, including a full TensorFlow model with trained weights, as well as BigQuery metadata, access lists, tenant logs, GKE cluster names, and internal container image paths.' This UC catches that fan-out — the service-agent reading data outside its expected project boundary. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/access-control
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1528
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Vertex AI Pipelines reading from a central feature-store project
  • AutoML training jobs ingesting public Google datasets from gs://gcs-public-data
  • Multi-region failover where the same service-agent fronts replicas in paired regions
  • Federated/AutoSxS evaluation jobs that read reference models from a shared eval project
Suppression filter
| where not(PrincipalEmail in ("<approved-central-feature-store-sa>")) and not(ResourceName startswith "projects/gcs-public-data")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull every action by the suspect service-agent in the last 24h; correlate with the time of any Model.upload from a suspect bucket (see the upload-mismatch UC) — if the cross-project access starts within minutes of an upload, treat as confirmed token theft. Step 2 — Contain: open a P1 with Google Cloud Support to invalidate the serving-container's metadata token and force redeploy, undeploy the affected model endpoint, and rotate any service-agent keys you can rotate yourself. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every BigQuery dataset / GCS bucket / GKE cluster the token touched, snapshot tenant audit logs for the impact window, and pivot on the attacker source IP for any other principals it authenticated as.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Cloud Platform", "Google Cloud Storage", "Google BigQuery")
| where AccountDisplayName has_any ("gcp-sa-aiplatform", "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com", "vertex-ai-serving")
| where ActionType has_any ("storage.objects.get", "storage.objects.create", "bigquery.tables.get", "bigquery.datasets.get", "container.clusters.list")
| extend TargetResource = tostring(ObjectName)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), DistinctTargets=dcount(TargetResource), SampleTargets=make_set(TargetResource, 10) by AccountDisplayName, ActionType
| where DistinctTargets > 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where PrincipalEmail has_any ("gcp-sa-aiplatform", "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com")
| where ServiceName in ("storage.googleapis.com", "bigquery.googleapis.com", "container.googleapis.com")
| extend CallerProject = extract(@"service-(\d+)@", 1, PrincipalEmail)
| extend TargetProject = tostring(parse_json(ResourceLabels).project_id)
| where isnotempty(CallerProject) and isnotempty(TargetProject) and CallerProject != TargetProject
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), DistinctTargets=dcount(ResourceName), Methods=make_set(MethodName) by PrincipalEmail, CallerProject, TargetProject
| where DistinctTargets > 2

CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Change.object) as objects from datamodel=Change where Change.user IN ("*service-*@gcp-sa-aiplatform*", "*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com") Change.action IN ("read","created","modified") by Change.user Change.src Change.dest 
| `drop_dm_object_name("Change")` 
| rex field=user "service-(?<caller_project_num>\d+)@" 
| rex field=dest "gs://(?<bucket>[^/]+)" 
| eval bucket_project_prefix=mvindex(split(bucket, "-"), 0) 
| stats min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime values(bucket) as buckets dc(bucket) as bucket_count by user caller_project_num 
| where bucket_count > 2 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Change.object) as objects from datamodel=Change where Change.user IN ("*service-*@gcp-sa-aiplatform*", "*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com") Change.action IN ("read","created","modified") by Change.user Change.src Change.dest 
| `drop_dm_object_name("Change")` 
| rex field=user "service-(?<caller_project_num>\d+)@" 
| rex field=dest "gs://(?<bucket>[^/]+)" 
| eval bucket_project_prefix=mvindex(split(bucket, "-"), 0) 
| stats min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime values(bucket) as buckets dc(bucket) as bucket_count by user caller_project_num

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning unexpected child process from Steam Workshop content directory AIInstallation High
Detects Wallpaper Engine (wallpaper32.exe / wallpaper64.exe) spawning a child process whose image resides under the Steam Workshop content directory for Wallpaper Engine (app id 431960). Per Kaspersky, malicious 'application'-type wallpapers auto-execute bundled payloads at install — this is the core execution telemetry shape. Rationale: Pulls the article's specific parent binaries (Wallpaper Engine's wallpaper32.exe/wallpaper64.exe) and the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop app id 431960 path. Cross-checked Steam app id from public Steam Wallpaper Engine page and SteamDB. Cross-checked against: • https://store.steampowered.com/app/431960/Wallpaper_Engine/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'application' wallpapers (system monitors, widget apps) installed by power users that the security team has not vetted
  • Wallpaper Engine self-update spawning its own installer from the Steam apps directory (parent path mismatch but similar shape)
  • Crash reporting via WerFault.exe being launched from the Workshop content folder
  • Developers testing their own Workshop submissions on dev workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","dllhost.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ChildImage SHA256/MD5 and cross-reference against the article's MD5 list and threat-intel; pull the Workshop content sub-folder (the numeric id after 431960 is the Workshop item id — look it up on steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=<id> to see the wallpaper name/author). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment, kill the child process tree, remove the Workshop subscription via steam://url/CommunityFilePage/<id> when ready. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256/MD5 across the fleet for other hosts with the same wallpaper, then run UC2/UC3/UC4 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload, Steam credential file access, C2 IPs) against the same DeviceId for the next 24h to surface follow-on stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where FileName !in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or CommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wallpaper Engine Spawning Child From Steam Workshop Content Directory
id: 5d7b5e4a-8a13-4d57-9e2c-31b8f1c4b2d4
description: Detects Wallpaper Engine spawning a child process whose image lives under the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop content folder (app id 431960).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains: '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
      - '\conhost.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_path and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\Wallpaper64.exe) (@Image:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\* OR @CommandLine:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\*) -@Image:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\conhost.exe OR *\WerFault.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ImageFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/conhost\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 path (Steam credential stealer sideload) AIInstallation High
Genuine AggregatorHost.dll ships in %WINDIR%\System32\. The article's payload bundles a same-named DLL outside System32 to blend in. Detects any process loading AggregatorHost.dll whose folder path is not the canonical System32 location. Rationale: Article names AggregatorHost.dll specifically as the sideloaded Steam credential stealer. Real AggregatorHost.dll is a tiny Windows .NET host stub in System32 — any other location is high-fidelity. MITRE T1574.002 mapping confirmed against attack.mitre.org. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running locally-built .NET-hosting code that names its host AggregatorHost.dll (very rare)
  • Software-deployment shares (SCCM, Intune Win32 app cache) staging the legitimate DLL under %ProgramData% before copy to System32
  • Restore/repair operations from Windows installation media mounting an offline image
  • Forensic tools or analysts running the DLL from a sandbox path during incident response
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded DLL, compare SHA256/MD5 to the known-bad list in UC5, and check signature with sigcheck/Get-AuthenticodeSignature — genuine AggregatorHost.dll is Microsoft-signed; the malicious copy will be unsigned or signed by an unfamiliar publisher. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loading process, quarantine the DLL file and its parent folder (likely a Workshop subfolder under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\). 3) Hunt: enumerate all DeviceFileEvents writes of AggregatorHost.dll in the last 30 days across the fleet, pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName to find every distinct dropper, and check for outbound network connections from the loading process to the article's C2 IPs.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source =~ "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[5].["#text"])
| extend ProcessImage = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[4].["#text"])
| extend ImageHashes = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[11].["#text"])
| where ImageLoaded endswith @"\AggregatorHost.dll"
| where ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessImage, ImageLoaded, ImageHashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AggregatorHost.dll Loaded From Non-System32 Path (Wallpaper Engine Sideload)
id: a3f1c4b2-7d8e-4f9a-9b1c-2d4e5f6a7b8c
description: Detects load of AggregatorHost.dll from any folder other than the canonical System32 / SysWOW64 / WinSxS paths, a sideload technique observed in the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine credential-theft chain.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\AggregatorHost.dll'
  filter_legit:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\'
      - 'C:\Windows\SysWOW64\'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:*\AggregatorHost.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\aggregatorhost.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\AGGREGATORHOST.DLL) -@ImageLoaded:(C\:\\Windows\\System32\\* OR C\:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\* OR C\:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*)
#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad OR #event_simpleName=ImageHash
| TargetFileName=/\\AggregatorHost\.dll$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/^C:\\Windows\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=7 ImageLoaded="*\\AggregatorHost.dll" NOT (ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\System32\\AggregatorHost.dll" OR ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\AggregatorHost.dll" OR ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*\\AggregatorHost.dll") | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Image) as loading_process values(Hashes) as dll_hashes count by host ImageLoaded User
Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files AIActions on Objectives High
Detects file reads or copies of Steam credential artefacts (ssfn* sentry files, loginusers.vdf, config.vdf) by processes that are not part of the Steam client family. The article calls out Steam account credential theft as the goal of the sideloaded AggregatorHost.dll. Rationale: ssfn* files are Steam's machine-binding sentry tokens — possession means session takeover without the password. loginusers.vdf holds the cached account list. Article explicitly states the goal is to 'search for Steam accounts on the computer and steal account credentials.' Cross-checked Steam credential artefact paths against public Steam Support documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://help.steampowered.com/en/faqs/view/65A9-CFE7-2369-A0A8 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/
ATT&CKT1555 T1539 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup utilities (Acronis, Veeam Agent, Macrium) capturing user profile data including the Steam config folder
  • AV/EDR products scanning the Steam config folder during a full filesystem sweep
  • Steam beta launcher variants or third-party Steam family-sharing tools that legitimately read ssfn files
  • Forensic acquisition tools (FTK Imager, KAPE) being run by IR or sysadmins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup.exe","veeamagent.exe","acronis_loader.exe","mscsweep.exe","MsMpEng.exe","kape.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName and its SHA256; if it's an unsigned binary under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is almost certainly the article's stealer. Grab a copy of the file for malware analysis. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-log out the affected Steam account via Steam Account Security (deauthorize all devices), invalidate the user's Steam password and Steam Guard recovery codes, and remove the malicious wallpaper Workshop subscription. 3) Hunt: pivot on the dropper SHA256 across the fleet, query UC2 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload) and UC4 (C2 connections) for the same host, and check Steam community trade/market activity for the user's account in the last 7 days for asset theft.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Steam\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
   or TargetFilePath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe"))
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\Steam\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Steam Process Accessing Steam Credential Artefacts
id: 7b9c1d2e-3f4a-5b6c-7d8e-9f0a1b2c3d4e
description: Detects file access to Steam sentry (ssfn*), loginusers.vdf, or config.vdf by processes outside the Steam client family — the credential-theft step of the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine campaign.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_files:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i)\\(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$'
  filter_steam:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\steam.exe'
      - '\steamservice.exe'
      - '\steamwebhelper.exe'
      - '\gameoverlayui.exe'
      - '\streaming_client.exe'
      - '\steamerrorreporter.exe'
  condition: selection_files and not filter_steam
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\loginusers.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\LoginUsers.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\config.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\Config.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\ssfn* OR @TargetFilename:*\Steam\config\*) -@Image:(*\steam.exe OR *\Steam.exe OR *\steamservice.exe OR *\steamwebhelper.exe OR *\gameoverlayui.exe OR *\GameOverlayUI.exe OR *\streaming_client.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\\loginusers\.vdf|\\config\.vdf|\\ssfn[0-9]+|\\Steam\\config\\)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client|steamerrorreporter)\.exe$/i
| NOT regex("\\\\Steam\\\\", field=ContextImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="loginusers.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="config.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="ssfn*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client)\.exe$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="loginusers.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="config.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="ssfn*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client)\.exe$")
Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) AICommand & Control High
Network beacon to the three article-named C2 endpoints used by the DarkKomet backdoor / AggregatorHost stealer / Lumma / Vidar / RanEngine payloads delivered through malicious Wallpaper Engine wallpapers. Any internal host contacting these is high-confidence compromise. Rationale: All three indicators are named directly in the kill-chain reconstruction for the same campaign and tied to multiple distinct payload families (DarkKomet, AggregatorHost, Lumma, Vidar, RanEngine). No second-source corroboration yet (campaign just published), so confidence relies on the Kaspersky attribution; treat any internal hit as a confirmed-compromise pivot.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation traffic from a security tool (e.g. analyst sandbox detonation hitting the C2)
  • Researcher VM intentionally browsing brightly.to for analysis
  • Shared-hosting provider parking the IP on an unrelated benign domain (verify reverse DNS)
  • Outbound proxy / SASE service health-checking a blocklisted URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","falcon-sensor.exe","sentinelagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which internal hosts connected and which user/process initiated; pull InitiatingProcessFileName & InitiatingProcessFolderPath — if process lives under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is the article's chain. 2) Contain: block 202.144.192.29, 120.48.156.17, and *.brightly.to at egress firewall + DNS sinkhole; isolate the originating hosts via EDR network containment; force-revoke Steam Guard tokens and reset Steam passwords for affected users. 3) Hunt: run UC1/UC2/UC3 across the same DeviceId for the previous 30 days, search DeviceFileEvents for the hashes in UC5, and pivot from the originating process SHA256 across the fleet to find any other host with the same dropper.
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2_IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2_Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr in (C2_IPs) or DstHostname in~ (C2_Domains) or Url has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process=tostring(parse_json("")), RemoteIP=DstIpAddr, RemoteUrl=coalesce(DstHostname, Url)),
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DnsQuery in~ (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process="", RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=DnsQuery),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP in (C2_IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2_Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, User=SourceUserName, Process=DestinationProcessName, RemoteIP=DestinationIP, RemoteUrl=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationDnsDomain))
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine Campaign C2 Connection

Known DarkKomet / Wallpaper-Engine campaign payload hash execution or write AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of any of the 13 article-named MD5s tied to the malicious wallpaper bundles (DarkKomet droppers, AggregatorHost.dll variants, Lumma/Vidar/RanEngine stages). Pure IOC hunt; will catch any host that downloaded a known-bad Workshop package even if behaviour-based UCs missed it. Rationale: All 13 MD5s are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle covering the DarkKomet droppers and AggregatorHost.dll sideload payloads. 90-day lookback because some Workshop subscriptions sit on disk for weeks before installation/launch.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or research VM in the fleet legitimately running known-bad samples
  • EDR / SOAR auto-detonation pipeline (e.g. ANY.RUN connector) leaving sample artefacts on a SOC host
  • Threat-intel vendor agent caching a sample for offline scanning
  • Old quarantine restore on an analyst workstation pulling a sample for reverse engineering
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hit isn't an analyst sandbox; pull DeviceName, FolderPath, parent process and timeline of the file write — chase upstream to find the wallpaper Workshop item id (the path under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\<id>\). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any running process matching the hash, quarantine the file system-wide via Defender Indicator (FileHash → BlockAndRemediate), push the 13 hashes to corporate AV/EDR blocklists. 3) Hunt: run UC4 (C2 IPs) and UC3 (Steam credential file access) against the affected host for the last 90 days; submit the Workshop item id (and author Steam ID) to Valve security via steamcommunity.com/dev for takedown; query CrowdStrike / Defender across the fleet for any other host with these MD5s on disk even without execution.
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceImageLoadEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DllLoad", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="Process", FileName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256),
    (ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where TargetFileMD5 in (BadMD5) or Hash in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="FileEvent", FileName=TargetFileName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, MD5=TargetFileMD5, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256),
    (SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where FileHash has_any (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Source="4688", FileName=NewProcessName, CommandLine=CommandLine, MD5=FileHash, SHA256="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
