Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("120.48.156.17", "202.144.192.29") or RemoteUrl has_any ("brightly.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["120.48.156.17", "202.144.192.29"]);

ImNetworkSession

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 19 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged multiple ClickFix campaigns that deliver three malware loaders called BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and Potemkin, per independent reports from Morphisec, BlueVoyant, and Huntress, respectively. Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix PowerShell paste-and-run from browser (Win+R lure) · [LLM] Potemkin chain: msiexec.exe spawning mshta.exe · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Lorem Ipsum Loader: outdated Node.js 7.10.1 executing JS payload · [LLM] Lorem Ipsum Loader DLL side-load via planted mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll · [LLM] Potemkin Loader victim-ID file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver · [LLM] BabaDeda Storage Crypter reads external payload List.Control.dat · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] RMMProject Chromium ABE bypass — non-browser access to Local State / Login Data · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
ClickFix PowerShell paste-and-run from browser (Win+R lure) AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickFix social-engineering primitive shared by all three campaigns: a browser process is the parent of powershell.exe with a one-liner that fetches a remote ZIP or executes inline. This is the entry point for BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and the Potemkin MSI dropper. Rationale: Article states all three campaigns begin with ClickFix lures that 'deceive users into running attacker-supplied PowerShell commands' — browser parent + interpreter child + remote-fetch verb is the signature shape. Cross-checked Morphisec, BlueVoyant, Huntress write-ups for the consistent browser-to-PowerShell paste pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/ • https://www.blueoyant.com/insights/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT support scripts that helpdesks email as one-liners users paste into PowerShell
  • Developer running `iwr | iex` to install dev tools (Chocolatey-style installs)
  • Browser extensions that legitimately spawn cmd.exe for native messaging hosts
  • QA automation that launches PowerShell via a custom URL handler
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","--app=","--enable-features") and ProcessCommandLine has "chocolatey.org")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull full ProcessCommandLine and the immediately-preceding 60s of browser DeviceNetworkEvents for the host — identify the lure URL the user visited. Capture the SHA256 of any child payload dropped. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the powershell.exe tree, and remove any scheduled task / Run-key persistence created in the last hour. Reset the user's credentials and revoke active sessions if browser-stored secrets were accessed. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org for the lure domain across DnsEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents, pivot on the dropped payload SHA256 across the fleet, and check EmailEvents for the lure delivery vector.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("iex","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","Net.WebClient","Start-BitsTransfer","-EncodedCommand","curl ","certutil -urlcache","FromBase64String")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("iex","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","Net.WebClient","Start-BitsTransfer","-EncodedCommand","curl ","certutil -urlcache","FromBase64String")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Browser-to-Interpreter Paste-and-Run
id: 9f1d6c2a-8e10-4f1f-b34a-2b4c91c5b001
description: Detects the ClickFix social-engineering chain where a browser process spawns PowerShell/cmd/mshta with a one-liner that pulls a remote payload.

  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html

tags:

  category: process_creation

detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_cmd:

      - 'Invoke-Expression'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'Net.WebClient'
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - 'certutil -urlcache'
      - 'FromBase64String'

Lorem Ipsum Loader: outdated Node.js 7.10.1 executing JS payload AIInstallation High
BlueVoyant documents that the Lorem Ipsum Loader chain drops an outdated Node.js binary (version 7.10.1 released in 2017) bundled in the ZIP and uses it to execute JavaScript payloads, evading modern AMSI/script-host telemetry. Hunts for any node.exe execution that does not come from a developer-installed location. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'an outdated version of Node.js released in 2017 (version 7.10.1)' bundled with the ZIP to execute JavaScript — node.exe from a non-developer path with a .js arg is a near-unique signature for this loader chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.blueoyant.com/insights/ • https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v7.10.1/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based desktop apps (VS Code, Slack, Discord) shipping their own embedded node.exe — generally live under \AppData\Local\<app>\ so add per-app allowlist
  • Portable Node installs in developer-chosen folders (e.g. C:\tools\node\)
  • CI/build runners that drop Node into a temp workspace
  • npm package post-install scripts that fork node from cache
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\", @"\AppData\Local\slack\", @"\AppData\Local\Discord\", @"\AppData\Local\GitHubDesktop\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Get the SHA256 + ProductVersion of node.exe; confirm it really is 7.10.1 (pre-AMSI-integrated). Pull the .js argument and dump its contents from the host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill node.exe tree, remove the originating ZIP and any persistence DLL-side-load directory (mscoree.dll / msvcp140.dll). Reset user credentials — Lorem Ipsum hands off to Rhysida ransomware operators. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep fleet for node.exe SHA256 7.10.1 hash, query DeviceFileEvents for that same hash being written, and pivot on the ParentBaseFileName to find the dropper that placed it.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js" or ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7.10"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\nodejs"
| where FolderPath !contains @"\nvm\" 
| where FolderPath !contains @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".js"
| where NewProcessName !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\nodejs\\"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\nvm\\"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\AppData\\Roaming\\npm\\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Lorem Ipsum Loader DLL side-load via planted mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll AIInstallation High
BlueVoyant describes a batch script that establishes persistence by launching a DLL side-loading chain to execute a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll, which decodes the embedded loader. Hunts for these two specific DLL names being written outside their legitimate system locations. Rationale: Article names the specific DLLs: 'a malicious DLL ("mscoree.dll" or "msvcp140.dll")' used in the Lorem Ipsum side-load chain — these are the exact two filenames the campaign places next to its legitimate-looking host EXE. Cross-checked against: • https://www.blueoyant.com/insights/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/ • https://hijacklibs.net/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Standalone .NET application installers that bundle their own msvcp140.dll into the app folder under \Program Files (typically excluded above)
  • Game launchers / Unity-based apps that drop msvcp140.dll next to game executables in user-folder installs
  • Visual Studio Build Tools redist copying msvcp140.dll into project output folders
  • Portable apps under \AppData\Local\Programs\<vendor>\ that ship msvcp140.dll
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Programs\", @"\Steam\steamapps\", @"\Epic Games\") and InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the dropped DLL; compare to clean Microsoft-signed copies (signature, FileVersion). Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote it and the legitimate-looking host EXE in the same folder. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, remove the side-load directory, kill any process loaded from it. Block the SHA256 in MDE custom indicators. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the SHA256 of the malicious DLL across DeviceImageLoadEvents to find every host that ever loaded it; check DeviceProcessEvents for the legitimate-looking host EXE that side-loaded the DLL to identify the full delivery chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("mscoree.dll","msvcp140.dll")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| where FolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft.NET\"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("mscoree.dll","msvcp140.dll")
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS"
| where TargetFilePath !contains "\\Microsoft.NET\\"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potemkin Loader victim-ID file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver AIInstallation High
Huntress documents that the Potemkin loader writes a unique per-victim UUID to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver and uses it for task polling against its DGA-derived C2. This single, masquerading filename is a high-fidelity host-based indicator of Potemkin infection. Rationale: Article cites Huntress: 'victim identification by means of a unique UUID value written to "%LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver"' — this exact filename in this exact location is essentially zero-false-positive; legitimate Hyper-V uses .vhd/.vhdx and never writes to LOCALAPPDATA. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/005/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1083 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Almost none — Hyper-V's per-user state lives in C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Hyper-V\, not LOCALAPPDATA
  • A red-team/IR tool deliberately mimicking the IOC for detection-engineering validation
  • A malware sandbox under analysis writing the file as part of a sample replay
  • Some Microsoft Sysinternals diagnostic tool with a coincidentally similar name (unknown to exist)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the file contents — it should be a UUID; capture it. Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName + ParentFileName that wrote it (the Potemkin loader itself or its loader DLL). Step 2 (contain): Isolate host immediately, kill the writing process tree, capture memory dump of the writer for reflective-loader extraction, block its SHA256 fleet-wide. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceNetworkEvents from the same DeviceId in the prior 24h for DGA-style domain lookups (DnsRequest for high-entropy or dictionary-word domains); pivot the UUID across any other observable C2 channels you have (proxy logs, NetFlow) to map every host beaconing with that same victim ID.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where FolderPath contains @"\AppData\Local\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where TargetFilePath contains "\\AppData\\Local\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potemkin chain: msiexec.exe spawning mshta.exe AIDelivery High
Huntress reports the Potemkin chain installs an MSI package that drops a previously undocumented loader via an HTA payload. The msiexec.exe → mshta.exe parent/child relationship is rare in production and is the specific tee-up of the Potemkin loader. Rationale: Article states Huntress detected a chain where 'a sophisticated attack chain that installs an MSI package, which then drops a previously undocumented loader codenamed Potemkin via an HTML Application (HTA) payload' — msiexec.exe directly spawning mshta.exe is rare in benign software (vendors normally use cmd or custom EXEs). Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/007/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1218.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise installers that bundle HTA UI launchers (rare — typically vendor-specific)
  • Manual admin troubleshooting where a sysadmin chains msiexec with a diagnostic HTA
  • Old InstallShield wizards that defer to mshta for splash screens
  • Custom in-house MSI packages built with WiX that invoke an HTA for post-install prompts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("InstallShield","WiX") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("splash","readme.hta","setup.hta"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull both ProcessCommandLine values — extract the MSI source URL/path and the HTA URL/path. Hash both. Check whether the MSI is signed and by whom. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill mshta.exe tree, remove the dropped MSI cache from %TEMP% / %WINDIR%\Installer\, block both MSI and HTA hashes fleet-wide. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep DeviceFileEvents for hyper-v.ver (the Potemkin victim-ID file) on the same host; check DeviceNetworkEvents 1h before the MSI for the delivery URL and pivot on it across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BabaDeda Storage Crypter reads external payload List.Control.dat AIInstallation High
Morphisec documents the BabaDeda chain uses a staged loader component dubbed Storage Crypter that reads payload material from external storage-like files such as 'List.Control.dat'. Hunts for any process accessing or writing this specific filename, which is the article's unique on-disk artifact. Rationale: Article quotes Morphisec naming the exact filename: 'reads the payload material from external storage-like files such as "List.Control.dat"' — bespoke filename with no legitimate software association. Cross-checked against: • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013/
ATT&CKT1027.013 T1140 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A custom enterprise application that coincidentally uses the same filename (extremely unlikely)
  • Red-team / purple-team validation runs that emulate BabaDeda's storage pattern
  • Malware-analysis sandbox replaying the sample
  • Forensic image being mounted by a DFIR tool that triggers file-event telemetry
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName accessing the file — this is the Storage Crypter side-loader. Capture the file, decode it if possible (Morphisec sample indicates simple XOR/RC4). Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the loader process, remove the side-load directory and the .dat file, block the loader's SHA256 across the fleet. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot ContextImageFileName SHA256 across all hosts; search the same DeviceId for outbound connections to DanaBot/SectopRAT infrastructure (article cites both as second-stage payloads) and for browser-credential / DPAPI access events indicating successful stealer execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "List.Control.dat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "List.Control.dat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RMMProject Chromium ABE bypass — non-browser access to Local State / Login Data AIActions on Objectives High
Huntress reports RMMProject performs browser credential theft 'by getting around Chromium's App-Bound Encryption (ABE) protections'. ABE bypass requires a non-browser process to read the encrypted Local State or Login Data files. Hunts for foreign processes touching these Chromium credential stores. Rationale: Article cites Huntress: RMMProject 'enable[s] remote screen control and browser credential theft by getting around Chromium's App-Bound Encryption (ABE) protections' — the ABE bypass requires reading Local State (which holds the encrypted master key) from a non-browser context. Verified against ATT&CK T1555.003 and recent Chromium ABE technical write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/heads/main/components/os_crypt/sync/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1140 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, LastPass) reading browser stores during import flows
  • Endpoint backup agents (Veeam, Druva, Backblaze) snapshotting user profile folders
  • Browser-history search tools (Everything, Recoll) indexing the SQLite databases
  • Enterprise DLP/DRM agents scanning user profiles for sensitive data
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("1Password.exe","Bitwarden.exe","LastPass.exe","KeePass.exe","KeePassXC.exe","DashlanePasswordManager.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName, its SHA256, signature status, and folder path — known password managers should be allowlisted; unsigned/unknown binaries from \AppData\Local\Temp\ or \ProgramData\ are high-priority. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the foreign process, force-rotate ALL stored credentials for the affected user (browser-stored passwords, OAuth refresh tokens), revoke active session tokens, reset Entra ID password. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot SHA256 across the fleet (look for the RMMProject DLL on other hosts); inspect DeviceNetworkEvents for exfiltration of the credential blob immediately following the read; check the same DeviceId for hyper-v.ver (Potemkin victim ID) to confirm the full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Local State","Login Data","Cookies","Web Data")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\", @"\Chromium\User Data\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Local State","Login Data","Cookies","Web Data")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\", "\\Microsoft\\Edge\\User Data\\", "\\BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser\\User Data\\", "\\Chromium\\User Data\\")
| where ActingProcessName !has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Foreign Process Reading Chromium Credential Stores (App-Bound Encryption Bypass)
id: 7e9c1d33-2b88-4f51-a73e-2b4c91c5b007
description: Detects non-browser processes accessing Chromium's Local State, Login Data, Cookies, or Web Data — the prerequisite for App-Bound Encryption bypass used by RMMProject (Potemkin chain).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/
author: Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\Local State'
      - '\Login Data'
      - '\Cookies'
      - '\Web Data'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
      - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
      - '\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\'
      - '\Chromium\User Data\'
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\vivaldi.exe'
      - '\explorer.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_path and not filter_browsers
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\Google\Chrome\User?Data\* OR @TargetFilename:*\Microsoft\Edge\User?Data\* OR @TargetFilename:*\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User?Data\*) (@TargetFilename:*\Local?State OR @TargetFilename:*\Login?Data OR @TargetFilename:*\Cookies OR @TargetFilename:*\Web?Data) -@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MSEdge.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe OR *\vivaldi.exe OR *\explorer.exe)
#event_simpleName=/^File(OpenInfo|Written)$/ TargetFileName=/\\(Google\\Chrome|Microsoft\\Edge|BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser|Chromium)\\User Data\\/i | TargetFileName=/(Local State|Login Data|Cookies|Web Data)$/i | NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|chromium|opera|vivaldi|explorer)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="Local State" OR Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Edge\\User Data\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser\\User Data\\*") NOT (Filesystem.process_name="chrome.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="msedge.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="brave.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="explorer.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="SearchProtocolHost.exe") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="Local State" OR Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Edge\\User Data\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser\\User Data\\*") NOT (Filesystem.process_name="chrome.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="msedge.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="brave.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="explorer.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="SearchProtocolHost.exe") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161") or RemoteUrl has_any ("malicious.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["malicious.site"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("malicious.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("malicious.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("malicious.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("malicious.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",

   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vLLM CVE-2026-48746 auth bypass via malformed Host header on /v1/* (`/` or `?` in Host) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-48746: HTTP requests to a vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint where the Host header carries reserved URL characters (`/`, `?`) that the attacker injects to make starlette's `URL(scope=scope).path` resolve to a non-`/v1` path while FastAPI routing still serves the `/v1` API. Targets vLLM 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0 directly exposed (no RFC-conforming reverse proxy in front). Rationale: Article body explicitly names the bypass primitive: 'an attacker to include special URL characters such as `/` or `?` in the Host: header'. Any inbound request to `/v1/*` with `/` or `?` in the Host header is RFC-7230-non-compliant and points directly at CVE-2026-48746 exploitation; the GHSA advisory itself is the authoritative second source for the affected range (vllm 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a virtual-host string containing a path segment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus, Tenable, Qualys) running the CVE-2026-48746 plugin
  • Pen-test / red-team reproducing the PoC during an authorised engagement
  • Old IIS server bug where Host header is set to URL fragment by a legacy client (rare)
  • Custom internal tooling that uses host:port/path style proxying
Suppression filter
// suppress known scanners and internal pen-test source ranges
| where SrcIp !in ("<vuln_scanner_ip>", "<redteam_jumphost_ip>")
| where HostHdr !startswith "qualys" and HostHdr !startswith "nessus"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on SrcIp — pull all /v1/* requests from that source in the last 24h, decode the Host header to see the injected path/query, check whether HTTP 200 responses followed (successful bypass) vs 4xx (blocked). 2. Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, take the vLLM instance off the internet (revoke NSG/SG public ingress) until you can place an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx, ALB) in front per the advisory's mitigation note. 3. Hunt: enumerate every vLLM deployment via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName=='vllm' and SoftwareVersion < 0.22.0, audit which are internet-facing without a reverse proxy, review their access logs for the same Host-header pattern across the last 30 days, and check the model/prompt logs for unexpected inference calls that may indicate model-theft or data-exfil during the bypass window.
// vLLM CVE-2026-48746 — Host header carrying / or ? against a vLLM /v1/* endpoint
// Path 1: nginx/vllm access logs shipped via Syslog
let vllm_syslog =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend HostHdr = extract(@'"Host:\s*([^"\r\n]+)"', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath)
    | where HostHdr matches regex @"[/?]"      // RFC 7230 forbids these in Host header
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIp, HostHdr, ReqPath, SyslogMessage;
// Path 2: CEF/WAF in front of vLLM
let vllm_cef =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/v1/"
    | where DestinationHostName matches regex @"[/?]"
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct;
union vllm_syslog, vllm_cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vLLM /v1/* API access without Authorization header on auth-configured instance AIExploitation Medium
Hunts requests to vLLM OpenAI-compatible API endpoints (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models, /v1/embeddings) that arrive without an Authorization: Bearer header on a deployment that has VLLM_API_KEY / --api-key set. Successful 200 responses under these conditions are a direct symptom of CVE-2026-48746 exploitation or other middleware misconfiguration. Rationale: Article states the bypass 'allows to use the API without providing the configured VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key'. Endpoint set is the documented OpenAI-compatible surface vLLM exposes under /v1. A 200 with no Authorization Bearer on these paths is the post-bypass signature; correlates the reviewer-suggested credential-access pivot to the article's specific endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/openai_compatible_server.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vLLM deployments intentionally running without API key (legitimate, no auth configured)
  • Health-check probes from Kubernetes liveness/readiness hitting /v1/models without auth
  • Internal monitoring tooling using IP allowlist instead of bearer auth
  • Load balancer health pings
  • Initial /v1/models discovery calls from approved client SDKs before they read the token from env
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<k8s_node_cidr>", "<healthcheck_lb_ip>")
| where SyslogMessage !contains "kube-probe"
| where SyslogMessage !contains "ELB-HealthChecker"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the target vLLM instance has VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key set (check systemd unit, docker-compose, or k8s manifest env) — if no API key is configured, this is by design, suppress and tag the host. 2. Contain: if API key IS configured, treat as confirmed bypass — block the source IP at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, restart vLLM, and front the listener with nginx per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: pull all /v1/chat/completions and /v1/completions bodies from the suspect window — look for prompts that exfiltrate system prompts, leak training data via membership inference, or attempt prompt injection chains. Check egress for the same source pulling /v1/models repeatedly (recon).
// vLLM /v1/* requests lacking Authorization: Bearer that succeeded (200)
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/v1/chat/completions","/v1/completions","/v1/models","/v1/embeddings")
| extend ReqMethod = extract(@'"(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ReqPath   = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Status    = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
| extend SrcIp     = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend HasAuth   = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where isnotempty(ReqPath)
| where Status == 200
| where HasAuth == false
| summarize Requests=count(), Paths=make_set(ReqPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIp, Computer
| where Requests >= 1
| order by Requests desc

vLLM 401/403 followed by 200 on /v1/* from same source IP within short window AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation timeline of CVE-2026-48746: an attacker first probes vLLM auth (receiving 401/403 because they have no token), then within a short window obtains 200 responses on the same /v1/* endpoints from the same source IP without ever presenting valid credentials. Encodes the failure→success transition the reviewer flagged. Rationale: Reviewer suggestion 3, anchored to the article's auth-bypass narrative. A single source IP receiving 401/403 then 200 on /v1/* within 10 minutes — without a credential change — is exactly the exploit timeline the article describes (probe → bypass via Host header → unauthorised inference). Time-window correlation cuts the broad 'no Authorization header' baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User mistyped API key, fixed it, and continued (legitimate fix)
  • Client SDK rotating to a freshly-issued token mid-session
  • Health probe failing then a real authenticated client succeeding shortly after (NAT/proxy sharing source IP)
  • Intermittent reverse-proxy auth header stripping on retry
  • CI pipeline fetching a token from a vault between failure and retry
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<corp_nat_gateway>", "<ci_runner_egress_ip>")
| extend FailHasToken = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where FailHasToken == false  // only the credential-less failure->success path
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the raw request lines for both the failing and succeeding calls from this SrcIp — compare the Authorization header values. If the failures had NO Authorization and the successes also had NO Authorization (or the same invalid one), this is the bypass; if the failures had an invalid token and successes had a valid one, it's a benign credential fix. 2. Contain: on confirmed bypass, block SrcIp at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, and deploy nginx in front per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: enumerate every /v1/chat/completions body from SrcIp in the success window, look for prompts probing internal data or system-prompt extraction; check whether SrcIp also performed Host-header injection (correlate to UC1) — co-occurrence is high-confidence exploitation evidence.
// Auth failure -> success transition on vLLM /v1/* from the same source IP within 10 min
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let vllm_reqs =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend Status  = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath) and isnotempty(SrcIp);
let failures =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (401, 403)
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, FailPath = ReqPath;
let successes =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (200, 201)
    | project SuccTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, SuccPath = ReqPath;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on SrcIp, Computer
| where SuccTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccTime, FailTime)
| summarize FailCount=count(), FirstFail=min(FailTime), FirstSuccess=min(SuccTime), Paths=make_set(SuccPath, 10) by SrcIp, Computer
| where FailCount >= 1
| order by FirstSuccess desc
