Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20131", "CVE-2023-36036")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20131", "CVE-2023-36036")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate

        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BleepingComputer
2026-06-16 5 use cases 0 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has given U.S. government agencies three days to secure their servers against an actively exploited vulnerability (CVE-2026-54420) in the LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] cPanel LiteSpeed Plugin Exploit Endpoint Hit (CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Symlink to cPanel/LiteSpeed Root-Owned Paths from Low-Privilege User (CageFS Escape) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CISA warns of another cPanel plugin flaw exploited in attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Root Shell or Persistence Tool Spawned by lsws/cpanel Plugin Parent (Post-Exploit)
cPanel LiteSpeed Plugin Exploit Endpoint Hit (CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172) AIExploitation High
Detects the LiteSpeed-published exploitation signature for the cPanel user-end plugin UNIX symlink-following vulnerability — requests calling the generateEcCert or packageUserSize JSON API functions, or cert_action_entry records referencing geneccert. These are the exact strings LiteSpeed told operators to grep for in /usr/local/cpanel/logs and /var/cpanel/logs. Rationale: Strings are taken verbatim from the LiteSpeed-published vulnerability check grep regex in the article: 'cpanel_jsonapi_func=(generateEcCert|packageUserSize)|cert_action_entry .*geneccert'. The vendor itself states any output is presumptive evidence of exploitation. Defender XDR / Falcon FDR don't ingest cPanel app logs natively, so endpoint-tier queries are omitted; CloudWatch is irrelevant unless logs are shipped to AWS — left empty.
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cPanel users with patched plugin (>= 2.4.8) running SSL/Let's Encrypt certificate-generation workflows — the same API endpoint is exercised
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys) probing for the CVE that mirror the exploit URL
  • Operator-run forensic grep against the same log paths echoing the strings into shell history that gets shipped to SIEM
  • Backup/log-shipping retries replaying historic log lines that contain the strings from a prior incident
  • cPanel plugin self-test suites that exercise the same JSON API endpoints during upgrade
Suppression filter
// Suppress patched hosts and known scanner sources
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert", "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"cert_action_entry\s+.*geneccert"
| where Computer !in (dynamic(["<patched-hosts-watchlist>"]))
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("<scanner-ip-allowlist>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the cPanel host's LiteSpeed user-end plugin version — anything < 2.4.8 plus a hit on these strings is presumptive compromise. Pull the requesting src IP, requesting cPanel user account, and exact URI from the access log; cross-reference against known scanner IP allowlists. Step 2 (contain): Force-update the LiteSpeed plugin to 2.4.8+ across all shared-hosting nodes, suspend the implicated cPanel user account, rotate that user's FTP/SSH/cPanel credentials, and snapshot the host for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2/UC3 — search the same host's process telemetry for `ln -s` into /usr/local/lsws or /usr/local/cpanel from the suspended user, then for any root-context process whose parent is an lsws or cpanel plugin binary in the same time window. Also check for new SUID files, /root/.ssh authorized_keys mutations, and unscheduled cron entries.
// cPanel JSON API exploit strings shipped via Linux Syslog agent
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert", "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"cert_action_entry\s+.*geneccert"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: cPanel LiteSpeed Plugin Exploit Attempt (CVE-2026-54420)
id: 5f8e4c3a-91d2-4b7a-9e6f-2c8a4d5e1b9f
description: Detects exploitation attempts against the LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin via the generateEcCert / packageUserSize JSON API endpoints used in the UNIX symlink-following privilege escalation chain (CVE-2026-54420, CVE-2026-48172).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-another-actively-exploited-cpanel-plugin-flaw/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_funcs:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert'
      - 'cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize'
  selection_cert:
    cs-uri-query|contains|all:
      - 'cert_action_entry'
      - 'geneccert'
  condition: selection_funcs or selection_cert
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate SSL certificate generation flows on patched (>= 2.4.8) LiteSpeed cPanel plugin
level: high
source:linux.syslog ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert" OR "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize" OR ("cert_action_entry" AND "geneccert"))

Symlink to cPanel/LiteSpeed Root-Owned Paths from Low-Privilege User (CageFS Escape) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the in-jail step of the CVE-2026-54420 chain: a low-privilege CageFS-confined user invoking ln -s to plant a symbolic link targeting /usr/local/lsws, /usr/local/cpanel, or /var/cpanel — the bait the vulnerable plugin then follows back into root-owned space. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact directories the LiteSpeed plugin reads when handling generateEcCert/packageUserSize. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit description of the bug — 'UNIX symlink following weakness' inside the LiteSpeed cPanel plugin escaping CloudLinux/CageFS isolation. The target directories /usr/local/lsws, /usr/local/cpanel, /var/cpanel are the canonical roots the plugin reads when handling the generateEcCert / packageUserSize endpoints UC1 alerts on; a symlink from a jailed user to those paths is the bait the bug follows. Excluding well-known service accounts cuts most operational noise without losing attacker signal.
ATT&CKT1548 T1068 T1222.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WHM/cPanel addon installers (Softaculous, Installatron, RVskin) symlinking templates into /var/cpanel during install
  • Reseller management scripts that link a customer's mailbox templates back into cPanel-owned spool dirs
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin troubleshooting where an operator su's to a customer account and creates a diagnostic symlink
  • cPanel transfer-tool restore operations linking restored backup paths into /var/cpanel
  • Custom plugin authors using ln -s as part of plugin self-registration under /usr/local/cpanel/3rdparty
Suppression filter
// Drop installer-pattern symlinks (Softaculous, Installatron, cPanel transfer tool)
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ln"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("/usr/local/cpanel/3rdparty/", "/scripts/restorepkg", "/usr/local/cpanel/whostmgr/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("softaculous","installatron","restorepkg","pkgacct")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the cPanel user who ran the ln -s, the exact link path created, and the symlink target. If the user is a real customer account (not a service/admin), and the target is a file the LiteSpeed plugin reads (cert configs, package metadata under those dirs), treat as a likely active exploit. Step 2 (contain): Suspend the customer account, capture the symlink and the link's parent directory for forensics, force LiteSpeed plugin upgrade to 2.4.8+, and audit /etc/passwd, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and crontabs for fresh modifications. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the symlink timestamp ±5 minutes with UC1 access-log hits from the same host, and run UC3 against the same time window to surface any root-context process spawned by lsws/cpanel binaries.
// Low-priv ln -s pointing at cPanel/LiteSpeed root-owned paths
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ln"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/ln" or ActingProcessName == "ln"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Root Shell or Persistence Tool Spawned by lsws/cpanel Plugin Parent (Post-Exploit) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation tell of CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172: a root-context shell, scripting interpreter, network tool, or account/key/cron utility whose parent is a binary under /usr/local/lsws/ or /usr/local/cpanel/. Article-specific because successful exploitation of the symlink-following bug yields root via the plugin's own process tree. Rationale: Anchored on the kill-chain Phase 3 detection hint: 'unexpected root-context process spawns parented by lsws/cpanel plugin binaries' — directly derived from the article's CloudLinux/CageFS-to-root escape narrative. The child binary set targets the textbook post-root actions Phase 5 calls out: 'new SUID binaries, cron entries, SSH key additions in /root or other users' ~/.ssh, and modifications to cPanel/WHM configuration files'. lsws and cpanel plugin binaries almost never legitimately fork interactive shells.
ATT&CKT1548 T1068 T1496 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WHM upcp (Update cPanel) running as root and invoking curl/wget for package downloads and chmod/useradd as it provisions
  • cPanel cron-tracker / chkservd spawning sh wrappers around health-check scripts
  • LiteSpeed licence renewal cron spawning curl to license.litespeedtech.com
  • WHM AutoSSL spawning ssh-keygen during account certificate provisioning
  • Admin manually running /scripts/restartsrv_* under WHM which fork bash subprocesses
Suppression filter
// Filter cPanel/LiteSpeed maintenance-update flows
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/lsws/", "/usr/local/cpanel/")
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","perl","python","python3","nc","ncat","socat","curl","wget","chmod","chown","useradd","usermod","passwd","ssh-keygen","crontab")
| where not(FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("license.litespeedtech.com","httpupdate.cpanel.net","securedownloads.cpanel.net","updates.cpanel.net"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("upcp","chkservd","cpkeyclt","autossl_check")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the exact child commandline. curl/wget to known cPanel/LiteSpeed licence/update endpoints (license.litespeedtech.com, httpupdate.cpanel.net, securedownloads.cpanel.net) is almost certainly maintenance; everything else — especially ssh-keygen, useradd, crontab editing /root or another user's crontab, chmod u+s — is presumptive compromise. Cross-reference timestamps with UC1 access-log hits and UC2 symlink-creation events on the same host. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep /etc/cron.d, /etc/crontab, /var/spool/cron, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, all user ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and find / -perm -4000 -newer <plugin install marker> across every co-tenant on the affected shared host; assume every co

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DragonForce BYOVD: Huawei/Topaz/K7/ToF drivers + ABYSSWORKER load for EDR kill · [LLM] Backdoor.Turn DLL sideload via legitimate VirtualBox/DbgView host + outbound TURN · [LLM] LimitBlankPassword LSA policy modified to enable network use of blank-password accounts · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Backdoor.Turn C2 over Microsoft Teams TURN relay (3478/3479/443 to MS IP from non-Teams) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DragonForce BYOVD: Huawei/Topaz/K7/ToF drivers + ABYSSWORKER load for EDR kill AIInstallation High
Hunts for creation or load of the specific vulnerable kernel drivers DragonForce abused in the Dec-2025 attack (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys, wsftprm.sys CVE-2023-52271, GameDriverx64.sys CVE-2025-61155, K7RKScan.sys CVE-2025-1055) plus ABYSSWORKER masquerading as a Palo Alto driver. These are the article's named BYOVD weapons used to terminate security tooling before ransomware deployment. Rationale: All four driver filenames and the ABYSSWORKER name are directly named in Symantec/BleepingComputer's writeup plus three CVEs (CVE-2023-52271, CVE-2025-61155, CVE-2025-1055). Driver files dropped to disk + service install of the same names is high fidelity since none of these drivers belong on a fleet endpoint. Cross-checked Loldrivers project list and CVE records. Cross-checked against: • https://www.loldrivers.io/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-52271 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1055
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate K7 Antivirus install on a managed endpoint (K7RKScan.sys is part of the K7 product)
  • Huawei laptop OEM-image deployment writing HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys
  • Tower of Fantasy game install on a corp gaming/test machine writing GameDriverx64.sys
  • Topaz signature pad driver install on a kiosk/POS host
  • Security researcher / red-team detonating loldrivers samples in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\K7 Computing" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Huawei" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Topaz Systems"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceFileEvents/DeviceImageLoadEvents for the host. Determine if the driver write/load came from a signed installer in Program Files (likely legit OEM) vs an unsigned process from a temp/Public/AppData path (suspicious). Pull SHA256 and check against LolDrivers known-bad list. 2) Contain: if path is non-standard or process is unsigned, isolate the host via Defender/Falcon network-contain, kill loaded service, block hash in EDR. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DeviceId for outbound TURN traffic (UC4), DbgView64.exe execution (UC2), and LimitBlankPasswordUse registry write (UC3). Sweep org for the same SHA256 in DeviceFileEvents over 30d.
let DriverNames = dynamic(["hwauidoos2ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","k7rkscan.sys","abyssworker"]);
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
    | where FileName has_any (DriverNames)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Source = "FileEvent";
let LoadHits = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName has_any (DriverNames)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName = "", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Source = "ImageLoad";
union FileHits, LoadHits
| order by Timestamp desc

Backdoor.Turn DLL sideload via legitimate VirtualBox/DbgView host + outbound TURN AIInstallation High
Hunts for execution of the legitimate signed VirtualBox or Sysinternals DbgView (specifically dbgview64.exe per the writeup) from non-Program-Files directories — the DragonForce delivery pattern where the signed host loads a malicious sideload DLL from the extracted ZIP. Also flags injection of Backdoor.Turn into dbgview64.exe. Rationale: Article specifies attacker downloaded a ZIP containing legitimate VirtualBox/DbgView + a malicious sideload DLL, and that Backdoor.Turn was injected into dbgview64.exe. Filtering signed-binary execution to non-Program-Files paths is the high-fidelity signal for portable-sideload hosts. Sysinternals/Oracle path allowlist suppresses dev workstations. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/ • https://lolbas-project.github.io/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmins running portable Sysinternals DbgView from a USB or network share for troubleshooting
  • QA team running portable VirtualBox.exe from a Downloads folder
  • Pentester / red-team using DbgView for kernel debug on a test box
  • Software developer extracting Oracle VirtualBox to a custom path
  • Vendor support engineer running VBoxManage.exe from a tool kit on a non-default path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe","ccmexec.exe","intune-managementextension.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent process — legitimate runs originate from explorer.exe (user double-click) or a known IT-deploy tool; suspicious runs originate from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or an unsigned extractor. Pull DLLs loaded by the host PID (DeviceImageLoadEvents) and check for unsigned DLLs from the same folder — classic sideload signature. 2) Contain: if a sideloaded unsigned DLL is loaded, isolate host, snapshot memory of dbgview64.exe for Backdoor.Turn IOCs, terminate the process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceId to the BYOVD driver detection (UC1), to UDP/3478 TURN traffic (UC4), and to LimitBlankPasswordUse registry change (UC3). Sweep org by SHA256 of the host binary's DLL neighbours.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("dbgview.exe","dbgview64.exe","virtualbox.exe","vboxmanage.exe","vboxsvc.exe")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox"
   and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Oracle\VirtualBox"
   and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Sysinternals"
   and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Debugging Tools"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dbgview64.exe","dbgview.exe","virtualbox.exe")
    | where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
    | project DeviceId, SideloadedDll = FileName, SideloadedDllPath = FolderPath, SideloadSha = SHA256
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, HostBinary = FileName, HostPath = FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SideloadedDll, SideloadedDllPath, SideloadSha
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("dbgview.exe","dbgview64.exe","virtualbox.exe","vboxmanage.exe","vboxsvc.exe")
| extend TargetProcessFolder = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "\\")[0])
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has @"C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox"
   and TargetProcessCommandLine !has @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Oracle\VirtualBox"
   and TargetProcessCommandLine !has @"C:\Program Files\Sysinternals"
   and TargetProcessCommandLine !has @"C:\Program Files\Debugging Tools"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash = SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sysinternals DbgView or VirtualBox Executed From Non-Standard Path
id: 2f8b1d54-7c19-4e2a-bc73-1a5d0e8f4926
description: Detects DragonForce's DLL sideload pattern — legitimate signed dbgview64.exe / VirtualBox binaries running from Temp / AppData / Public / Downloads / ProgramData rather than Program Files, indicating a portable copy used as a sideload host.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:

      - '\dbgview.exe'
      - '\dbgview64.exe'
      - '\VirtualBox.exe'
      - '\VBoxManage.exe'
      - '\VBoxSVC.exe'
  selection_path:

level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) (@Image:(*\dbgview64.exe OR *\DbgView64.exe OR *\dbgview.exe OR *\DbgView.exe OR *\VirtualBox.exe OR *\virtualbox.exe OR *\VBoxManage.exe) OR @NewProcessName:(*\dbgview64.exe OR *\DbgView64.exe OR *\VirtualBox.exe)) (@Image:(*\Temp\* OR *\AppData\* OR *\Users\Public\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\ProgramData\* OR *\PerfLogs\*) OR @NewProcessName:(*\Temp\* OR *\AppData\* OR *\Public\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\ProgramData\*)) -@Image:(C:\Program?Files\Oracle\VirtualBox\* OR C:\Program?Files?(x86)\Oracle\VirtualBox\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(dbgview64?|virtualbox|vboxmanage|vboxsvc)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(Temp|AppData|Public|Downloads|ProgramData|PerfLogs)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\(Oracle\\VirtualBox|Sysinternals|Debugging Tools)\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

LimitBlankPassword LSA policy modified to enable network use of blank-password accounts AIInstallation High
Detects modification of HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\LimitBlankPasswordUse to 0 — the article calls out DragonForce abusing this security policy to make rogue blank-password accounts usable over the network. By default Windows sets this to 1 (blank-password accounts are local-console only); flipping to 0 is a deliberate weakening of the auth boundary. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'LimitBlankPassword' Windows security policy abuse by DragonForce to make rogue users usable. Default Windows value is 1; an observed write of 0 to this specific registry path is extremely rare in a managed environment — single event is high fidelity. No CIS/STIG baseline sets this to 0. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/accounts-limit-local-account-use-of-blank-passwords-to-console-logon-only
ATT&CKT1112 T1078.003 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured GPO from a legacy domain still pushing the value (rare)
  • Sysadmin testing local account behaviour in a lab
  • Old security baseline rollback during a misguided remediation
  • Vendor installer that incorrectly toggles the LSA policy (very rare — would be a CVE-worthy bug)
  • Manual reg.exe / Set-ItemProperty from an interactive admin troubleshooting session
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpsvc.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !=~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — reg.exe, powershell.exe, secedit.exe under an admin session is suspicious; gpsvc.exe receiving from a legitimate GPO is benign (correlate against AD GPO change events). Check the timing against any change-management ticket. 2) Contain: revert the value to 1 via GPO or local reg push, isolate the host, audit local account creation events (4720) and group membership changes (4732/4728) on that DeviceId in the prior 24h. 3) Hunt: enumerate all local accounts with blank or weak passwords (`net user`), sweep the org for the same registry value across 30d, and pivot to UC1/UC2/UC4 detections on the same DeviceId.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "LimitBlankPasswordUse"
| where RegistryValueData == "0" or RegistryValueData == "0x0" or RegistryValueData == "0x00000000"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, PreviousRegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated","Set")
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa"
| where RegistryValue =~ "LimitBlankPasswordUse"
| where RegistryValueData in ("0", "0x0", "0x00000000")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, RegistryPreviousValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor.Turn C2 over Microsoft Teams TURN relay (3478/3479/443 to MS IP from non-Teams) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for the article's signature C2 channel — outbound UDP/3478-3481 or TCP/443 to Microsoft Teams TURN relay infrastructure from a process that is NOT the Teams client. Backdoor.Turn obtains an anonymous Teams visitor token and tunnels C2 through legitimate MS TURN servers, so the host process binding the socket should never be teams.exe / ms-teams.exe. Rationale: Article's central novel TTP: 'Backdoor.Turn is the first known in-the-wild malware to abuse Microsoft Teams TURN relays for C2', specifically obtaining anonymous Teams visitor tokens and connecting via legitimate MS TURN. Detection logic — non-Teams process binding to TURN ports / Teams TURN hostnames — directly maps to that. Cross-checked against Praetorian 'Ghost Calls' research which used the same primitive in 2025. Cross-checked against: • https://www.praetorian.com/blog/ghost-calls-abusing-web-conferencing-infrastructure/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/prepare-network • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/002/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom enterprise VoIP/SIP client legitimately using STUN/TURN on 3478
  • WebRTC-based apps (Slack Huddles, Zoom, Discord) traversing 3478 to non-Microsoft TURN servers — usually filterable but watch RemoteUrl
  • Internal NAT-traversal tooling used by remote-access products (TeamViewer, AnyDesk) when they fall back to STUN
  • Browsers (chrome.exe, msedge.exe) running Teams web client — should still be filtered by hostname/Teams cookie path but can be noisy
  • Network test tools (stuntman, coturn-client) used by network engineers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("slack.exe","zoom.exe","discord.exe","webex.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\TeamViewer\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AnyDesk\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the initiating process binary, its SHA256, signing status, and folder. Legitimate Teams traffic always originates from Teams.exe under Program Files\WindowsApps or Microsoft\Teams\current; any other process bound to 3478 is the lead. Decode the visitor-token request (HTTPS to *.teams.microsoft.com/anonymousjoin) in proxy logs if available. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, dump memory of the suspect process for Go-runtime strings (RAT was Go-based per article) and TURN credentials, block the C2 destination IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceId to UC2 (dbgview64.exe) and UC1 (BYOVD drivers) — if those fire on the same host, treat as confirmed DragonForce. Sweep org for the same destination IP/hostname pattern over 30d and for processes that issued TURN allocation requests but lack a teams.exe parent.
let TURNPorts = dynamic([3478,3479,3480,3481]);
let TeamsBinaries = dynamic(["teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","msteams.exe","microsoft.teams.exe"]);
let TeamsHosts = dynamic(["turn.teams.microsoft.com","worldaz.tr.teams.microsoft.com","relay.teams.microsoft.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where (Protocol =~ "Udp" and RemotePort in (TURNPorts))
   or (RemotePort == 443 and (RemoteUrl has_any (TeamsHosts) or RemoteUrl endswith ".teams.cloud.microsoft"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (TeamsBinaries)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft\Teams\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\MSTeams"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), DistinctRemotes = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleUrl = any(RemoteUrl)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where ConnCount >= 3
| order by ConnCount desc
let TURNPorts = dynamic([3478,3479,3480,3481]);
let TeamsBinaries = dynamic(["teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","msteams.exe","microsoft.teams.exe"]);
let TeamsHostnames = dynamic(["turn.teams.microsoft.com","worldaz.tr.teams.microsoft.com","relay.teams.microsoft.com"]);
let TeamsRunningHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName has_any (TeamsBinaries)
    | summarize TeamsLastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (NetworkProtocol =~ "UDP" and DstPortNumber in (TURNPorts))
   or (DstPortNumber == 443 and (DstHostname has_any (TeamsHostnames) or DstHostname endswith ".teams.cloud.microsoft"))
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), DistinctRemotes = dcount(DstIpAddr), SampleRemote = any(DstIpAddr), SampleHostname = any(DstHostname)
          by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| join kind=leftouter TeamsRunningHosts on DvcHostname
| where isempty(TeamsLastSeen) or LastSeen > TeamsLastSeen + 1h
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, ConnCount, Ports, DistinctRemotes, SampleRemote, SampleHostname, TeamsLastSeen
| order by ConnCount desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender) @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:(3478 OR 3479 OR 3480 OR 3481) OR (@DestinationPort:443 AND @DestinationHostname:(*.teams.microsoft.com OR *.teams.cloud.microsoft OR worldaz.tr.teams.microsoft.com))) -@Image:(*\teams.exe OR *\Teams.exe OR *\ms-teams.exe OR *\msteams.exe OR *\Microsoft.Teams.exe) -@Image:(*\Microsoft\Teams\* OR *\WindowsApps\MSTeams*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=3478 OR RemotePort=3479 OR RemotePort=3480 OR RemotePort=3481 OR (RemotePort=443 AND ContextImageFileName!=/\\(teams|ms-teams|msteams)\.exe$/i))
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(teams|ms-teams|msteams|Microsoft\.Teams)\.exe$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(Microsoft\\Teams|WindowsApps\\MSTeams)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=ConnCount))
| ConnCount >= 3

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.transport) as transport from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3478,3479,3480,3481) OR (All_Traffic.dest_port=443 AND (All_Traffic.dest="*.teams.microsoft.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.teams.cloud.microsoft" OR All_Traffic.dest="worldaz.tr.teams.microsoft.com"))) NOT All_Traffic.app IN ("teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","msteams.exe","Microsoft.Teams.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("62.164.177.25", "192.36.27.51") or RemoteUrl has_any ("projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["62.164.177.25", "192.36.27.51"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase

tags:

logsource:

detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'

    selection_domain:

            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'

falsepositives:

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("62.164.177.25", "192.36.27.51")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("62.164.177.25", "192.36.27.51")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]

        where DNS.query IN ("projetosmecanicos.com.br", "socialbizsolutions.com", "professionalhomebasedbusiness.com", "safefire.jo", "glanz-gmbh.de", "turnkeyaiagents.com", "comunidadesparentais.com.br", "mysimerp.net")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0) AIWeaponization High
Detects installation or invocation of google-cloud-aiplatform Python SDK at versions 1.139.0 through 1.147.x, which silently fall back to an attacker-owned GCS bucket via the deterministic `<project>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern when no explicit staging bucket is supplied. Catches both first-time installs and runtime use of vulnerable libraries that should be upgraded to ≥1.148.0. Rationale: Pins to the EXACT vulnerable SDK version range disclosed in the Unit 42 article (1.139.0 — 1.147.x; fixed in 1.148.0 released 2026-04-15). The version regex eliminates noise from already-patched installs. Catches both interactive pip installs and CI/CD pipelines pulling pinned vulnerable versions. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://pypi.org/project/google-cloud-aiplatform/#history
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data science teams legitimately running pinned but outdated SDK versions in research notebooks
  • CI/CD pipelines re-installing an old pinned version in lockfiles awaiting upgrade
  • Docker image rebuilds replaying historical pip install commands from cached layers
  • Developers reproducing a known issue against a specific old SDK version for support tickets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","buildkitd.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","download","--no-deps"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and pull the full pip-install context — is this a developer workstation, build agent, or production ML pipeline? Check whether the SDK is actively used (search for `aiplatform.Model.upload` calls in the same project). 2) Contain: force-upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform to ≥1.148.0 in the affected environment; if the host has uploaded models in the last 7 days, treat any default-named staging buckets as suspect and verify ownership via `gcloud storage buckets describe`. 3) Hunt: pivot to GCS audit logs for any bucket matching `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` and confirm the bucket resides in the customer's own project, not an attacker-controlled one. Check Vertex AI Model Registry for models uploaded during the vulnerable window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn, VulnerableVersion, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pip3.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python3.exe"
| where CommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, CommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, VulnerableVersion, CommandLine, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access AIDelivery Medium
Hunts GCP audit logs for storage operations on buckets matching the deterministic `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern where the acting identity is NOT the customer's Vertex AI P4SA (`service-<project-num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) or a known internal pipeline service account. Surfaces both cross-tenant bucket squatting and unexpected writes that could be model-artifact poisoning. Rationale: Targets the exact bucket-name pattern from the article (`staging_bucket_name = project + "-vertex-staging-" + location`). Filtering OUT the legitimate Vertex AI P4SA isolates the access path the attacker would use — either bucket-squatting from a different project or an unexpected internal principal touching the staging bucket. Sigma omitted because this requires aggregation/exclusion logic not expressible as single-event-shape. Falcon/Defender/CloudWatch empty because this is GCP-native telemetry with no Falcon FDR or Microsoft endpoint equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-agents
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1525 T1530
Data sourcesWeb Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Customer DevOps service account legitimately reading the staging bucket during pipeline orchestration
  • Terraform/IaC service account creating or auditing the bucket during infra provisioning
  • Cloud Storage Transfer Service or Backup service principals enumerating buckets
  • Internal user using `gcloud storage` CLI for ad-hoc model artifact inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bucket ownership with `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket>` — if the project_number doesn't match your project, you've been squatted; treat as confirmed. Inventory any model artifacts already staged there. 2) Contain: immediately delete and recreate the bucket explicitly under your project, then upgrade the SDK to ≥1.148.0 across all clients. Revoke any models uploaded during the vulnerable window from the Vertex AI Model Registry and redeploy from a verified source. 3) Hunt: pull Vertex AI deployment events for the affected region and inspect model artifacts (`gsutil cat gs://<bucket>/.../model.joblib | python -c 'import pickletools; pickletools.dis(...)'`) for `__reduce__` payloads. Check IAM audit logs for any new permissions granted to external principals.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ServiceName == "storage.googleapis.com"
| extend BucketName = extract(@"projects/_/buckets/([^/]+)", 1, tostring(ResourceName))
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)"
| extend Principal = tostring(AuthenticationInfo.principalEmail)
| where Principal !endswith "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(MethodName), Principals=make_set(Principal), EventCount=count() by BucketName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.serviceName:storage.googleapis.com @protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-* -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
