Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SprySOCKS DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys) write / image load on Windows endpoint · [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_DRV IFEO persistence on vds.exe · [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence as Windows Print Processor (VSPMsg) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SprySOCKS DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys) write / image load on Windows endpoint AIInstallation High
Hunts for the WIN_DRV stage-zero driver 'fsdiskbit.sys' (DriverLoader) being dropped to disk or loaded as an image. fsdiskbit.sys is signed with a leaked certificate from the GitHub PastDSE project and is the loader that maps the in-memory RawWNPF rootkit driver. The filename is article-specific and not associated with any benign vendor. Rationale: fsdiskbit.sys and the DriverLoader designation are explicitly named in the ESET-sourced article body as the WIN_DRV first-stage. Filename has no overlap with legitimate Microsoft / vendor drivers per public driver databases. Earth Lusca/FishMonger attribution corroborated via ESET Operation FishMedley write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/i/earth-lusca-employs-new-linux-backdoor.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1553.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected with this exact filename — fsdiskbit.sys is not a known benign Windows driver
  • Forensic analyst extracting the IOC for sandboxing (use case context will explain)
  • Threat intel team copying the file to a malware library share
  • EDR live-response retrieval of the artifact for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull SHA256 of fsdiskbit.sys; check signer (PastDSE cert thumbprint) via DeviceFileCertificateInfo; confirm the file is signed by a non-MS cert and the writing process is not a known security tool. 2) Contain: Isolate host via MDE live response, block the SHA256 across the org, terminate any process loading the driver and capture a memory image for the RawWNPF in-memory driver. 3) Hunt: Pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet, look for IFEO\\vds.exe persistence (companion UC), VSPMsg print-processor registration, and outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket beacons from svchost / print spooler children.
let lookback = 14d;
let driverWrites = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let driverLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=tostring(""), InitiatingProcessAccountName;
driverWrites
| union driverLoads
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where TargetFileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:
    - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/windows-version-of-sprysocks-linux-malware-used-to-attack-govt-orgs/

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\fsdiskbit\.sys$/i

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV IFEO persistence on vds.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts for Image File Execution Options registry-key writes targeting vds.exe (Virtual Disk Service) — the IFEO-hijack persistence path used by SprySOCKS WIN_DRV to launch DriverLoader. ESET explicitly names vds.exe as the IFEO debugger target. Rationale: vds.exe IFEO is named verbatim in the article as the WIN_DRV persistence mechanism. IFEO writes targeting a specific binary like vds.exe are extremely rare in normal use — Application Verifier and AppCompat are the only common writers, neither targets vds.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/
ATT&CKT1546.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer enabling Application Verifier against vds.exe (extremely rare)
  • WinDbg gflags being set during driver debugging by a Microsoft support engineer
  • Endpoint hardening tool writing MitigationOptions to multiple system binaries (would hit other binaries too — pivot on whether vds.exe is the only target)
  • Manual VSS / disk troubleshooting where an admin attached a debugger
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("verifier.exe","gflags.exe","appverif.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/enable","-enable"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect RegistryValueData — if it points to a non-Microsoft-signed binary in C:\\Windows\\System32 / C:\\ProgramData / user-writeable path, treat as confirmed. Pull SHA256 of the debugger image. 2) Contain: Delete the IFEO Debugger value, isolate the host, block the debugger SHA256. Note vds.exe runs as SYSTEM when storage operations occur, so privesc has already happened. 3) Hunt: Search the fleet for the same RegistryValueData path, look for companion fsdiskbit.sys writes and VSPMsg print-processor registrations.
let lookback = 30d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"Image File Execution Options\vds.exe"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("Debugger","GlobalFlag","VerifierDlls","MitigationOptions","ReportingMode")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RegistryKey has @"Image File Execution Options\vds.exe"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("Debugger","GlobalFlag","VerifierDlls","MitigationOptions")

SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence as Windows Print Processor (VSPMsg) AIInstallation High
Hunts for registration of a Print Processor named VSPMsg under the Print Environments registry tree — the persistence mechanism used by SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS to load its DLL into spoolsv.exe at SYSTEM. The processor name VSPMsg is article-specific. Rationale: The processor name VSPMsg is explicitly called out in the article as the SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence registration. Print Processor registrations are rare overall and the specific VSPMsg name carries no legitimate vendor association. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/
ATT&CKT1547.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate printer driver vendor (HP/Canon/Brother) registering a new processor — name will not be VSPMsg
  • MSI-based printer driver install via msiexec.exe (filtered by InitiatingProcessFileName)
  • Sysadmin running prndrvr.exe to install drivers (filtered)
  • Windows Update servicing the spooler (rare, runs as TrustedInstaller)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","prndrvr.exe","setup.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and not (RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read RegistryValueData — the value will be the DLL filename of the Print Processor. Pull SHA256 and signer of that DLL from DeviceFileEvents / DeviceImageLoadEvents in C:\\Windows\\System32\\spool\\prtprocs\\. 2) Contain: Stop the Print Spooler service, remove the registry key and the dropped DLL, isolate the host. Spooler runs as SYSTEM so privesc has occurred. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the DLL hash org-wide, look for spoolsv.exe spawning unexpected children, outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket beacons from spoolsv.exe, and companion fsdiskbit.sys / IFEO\\vds.exe persistence on the same host.
let lookback = 30d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has @"\Print Processors\"
| where RegistryKey has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueName =~ "Driver"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("spoolsv.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","prndrvr.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has @"\Print Processors\"
| where RegistryKey has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hosts vulnerable to CVE-2023-24932 with internet exposure (SprySOCKS UEFI bootkit pre-position) AIWeaponization Medium
Posture hunt for endpoints still vulnerable to CVE-2023-24932 (BlackLotus / Secure Boot bypass), the flaw ESET telemetry suggests SprySOCKS may exploit as a UEFI bootkit component. Prioritises internet-facing devices that match the campaign's government-org targeting profile. Rationale: CVE-2023-24932 is explicitly named in the article as the Secure Boot flaw the suspected UEFI bootkit component might exploit. The vulnerability requires an active mitigation step (revocation) beyond the May 2023 patch; many fleets still carry vulnerable bootmgr versions. Cross-checked Microsoft MSRC advisory and Huntress threat library. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-24932 • https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/vulnerabilities/cve-2023-24932
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched hosts where the May 2023 KB is installed but the Secure Boot revocation step (KB5025885 manual step) has not been applied — TVM correctly flags these as still-vulnerable
  • Servers where reboot has been deferred indefinitely
  • Air-gapped / standalone devices that haven't pulled the revocation update
  • Hosts whose UEFI firmware doesn't support the DBX revocation update yet
Response runbook
1) Triage: Filter the result set to internet-facing assets and government-org-priority workloads (foreign-affairs, telecom, defence). Confirm KB5025885 (or successor) status. 2) Contain: Apply the manual Secure Boot revocation steps per KB5025885 starting with internet-facing tier-0 assets; reboot in maintenance window. Enable HVCI + Memory Integrity where missing. 3) Hunt: On all CVE-2023-24932-vulnerable hosts, search DeviceFileEvents for fsdiskbit.sys writes, DeviceRegistryEvents for IFEO\\vds.exe and Print\\Environments\\VSPMsg entries, and DeviceEvents for ActionType 'DeviceBootIntegrityChanged' or unexpected EFI partition writes.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
